ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: the trade screen
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Every trade opens in Rimfolk's own trade window: two lists, your goods to sell and the trader's to buy, side by side or as tabs; each price against the usual price, a grade for each good, the best deals both ways, every column sortable, and what the deal comes to. The prices, counts and Accept are the game's own, and the game's screen, with its sorts, marks and buttons, is one click away. Nothing is traded until you press Accept.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Rimfolk's own trade window and each part of the game's screen have their own switch under What's on, Trade screen. The window, the marks, the buttons, the readouts, the market card and the trade record are deeper game hooks; the sorts are the game's own kind of sort and work without them.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: It works the same for every trade: a trader or visitor on the map, a guest, a caravan at a town or met on the road, a ship called on the comms console. The advice comes from what Rimfolk already knows of the colony: the plan ahead's stock targets and food days, its shopping list, the blueprints, the journey being packed, the colonists' wishes, the drug policies and the research under way. Only what the colony has and can use counts as a need, so a tribe is told a tribe's needs.

points.li: Two lists, Ours to sell and Theirs to buy: side by side when the window is wide enough, else as two tabs, Sell and Buy. The button above the lists chooses: by width, always side by side, or always tabs; your choice and the tab you looked at are kept for the next trade.

Each list is grouped under the kinds of good (food, medicine, raw materials and so on), and each good has its picture and whole name, how many there are, the price with its mark against the usual, the deal's grade, what the colony needs of it, and how many to sell or buy. Point at a good for the rest: its market value and mass, the price's share of the value and the game's own reckoning, why the deal is called what it is, and what the colony uses it for.

The arrows point where the goods go: in the sell list > sells one more and < takes one back, in the buy list < buys one more and > puts one back. Ten with Shift and a hundred with Ctrl, a double arrow all or none, and a number can be typed, within the game's own limits. A trade either buys or sells a good: one being bought says so in the sell list, and a click takes it out of the purchase. Every price is the game's own for your negotiator, so the price shown is the price paid.

Game's screen, at the top, switches to the game's own trade screen for the same trade and counts; a small button beside its sort menus comes back. Trade Helper's panel and the old marks are there. Give gifts opens the game's screen in its gift mode; a trade in favor keeps the game's screen.

Accept is the game's own: it asks first when the trader is short of silver, tells you when the colony can't pay, and hands the goods over by pod or into the caravan. A caravan's mass, speed and days of food after the trade are the game's own strip at the top.
If the window can't be drawn, the game's screen takes the trade over on the same counts.

li.heading: Above or under, and the grades

points.li: Under each price, its mark against the usual price a trader pays or asks for your negotiator and difficulty: an arrow up when above it and down when under, and how far, in green when better for you and orange when worse. The good's tooltip gives the price's share of its market value too. Against market value alone a sale is always under and a purchase always over; the usual price is what shows a trader paying more, or asking less, than traders do.
Each good gets a grade in each list it is in, in words and in bars (three, two, one, none): great a fifth better than the usual price, good 7% better, fair within 7% of it, poor worse.

Vanilla Trading Expanded's market moves a grade a step: up for a sale at its highest of 60 days or of a good falling fast, and for a buy at its lowest or of a good rising fast; down at the other ends. The colony's own record moves it a step too: up for a price better than its best of the last 15 days, down for one a tenth worse.

Something the colony has no use for is never a good buy however cheap, and selling what it is short of or keeps all of is never a good sale. The good's tooltip gives its grade, why, and the advice's own reasons.

With Vanilla Trading Expanded, the market card beside a good's tooltip shows its market value now against its usual worth and against its average of the last 30 days, and its last days drawn, with the change (in the tooltip's words when the card is off).

li.heading: Best deals, sorting and the summary

points.li: Best deals, on the right: the top five sells and the top five buys graded good or great. A click finds the good in its list, on its tab.

Each column's header sorts its list under the kinds, the highest first or from A, and again the other way; the menu at the count's heading also sorts by market value, the market, its trend and mass. A search, a chip for each kind of good the trade has (food, medicine, raw materials, manufactured, weapons, apparel, art and books, drugs, animals, people, other), and Only in the deal narrow both lists.

This deal: what you sell and buy, its market value and the share of it paid; the net silver; the deal against the usual prices, as "about 12% better for you"; both ways by market value; the days of food at home after the trade; and Vanilla Trading Expanded's word when a big trade may move a price. Each side's silver now and after the trade is at the foot, beside Fill suggested, Clear suggested, Reset, Accept and Cancel.
At 1280 pixels wide the lists are tabs, each with all its columns; chosen side by side there, the need and how many there are give way first, and what they say stays in the tooltip.

li.heading: Sorting by price on the game's screen

points.li: On the game's own screen, its two "Sort by" menus gain five sorts, each the highest first: trader pays, trader asks (the prices for this negotiator, as the price columns show them, not the market value), price per kg (for a caravan's load), best deal, and suggested first.

The best deal is the price against the usual one: what a trader usually pays is 60% of a thing's worth and what it asks 140%, each moved by your negotiator. A sale a fifth above the usual is a good sale; a price a fifth under it is a bargain.
A good with nothing on that side (none of it to sell, or none at the trader) goes last. The caravan and transport pod windows share these menus; there Rimfolk's sorts are left out.

Of each good the colony keeps its need and as much again. The need is what it used in a season (15 days) by its own record, or a floor for its kind, the larger: 50 a person of wood, metal and stone blocks (250 at least), 25 of cloth and leather (75 at least), 3 of components (8 at least) and of medicine (6 at least), 5 of gold, jade and the like (20 at least).

Food goes by days of eating: the days the plan ahead keeps in store and the days ahead with nothing growing, 10 at least, raw food counted as the meals it cooks into. Medicine also keeps the plan ahead's own target where that is more.

On top, what is set aside: the blueprints' and frames' materials, a journey's packing, something promised for a wish or given for one, a season of what the drug policies schedule and what they carry, and a caravan's own food and medicine. A good with none of these rules (art, body parts, books) is never called more than needed.
Weapons and clothes go by spares: the best one of a kind for every three people. A copy worse than the best one kept is a worse spare.

Worth selling (pointing down): what is beyond what the colony keeps, things no one here can use (clothes no one can wear, a weapon biocoded to someone gone, a techprint already learned, a drug taken for pleasure that no drug policy allows), the worse spares, and a price a fifth above the usual on what is beyond the need alone.

Worth buying (pointing up), the most pressing first: food short of its days, medicine, feed for the animals fed from the stores, what the blueprints lack and the plan ahead's shopping list, components where machines break down, a contract that pays well, a colonist's open wish, a techprint or a book for the research under way, and a bargain on a stock the colony keeps that runs low.
Kept (a pin): something of it is set aside. The pin turns red when the trade sells into it.

Each mark's tooltip says why in numbers, and how the trader's price stands against the usual. In Rimfolk's window the same advice is the Need column of the buy list and the Keep column of the sell list (short, spare or kept), its reasons on the good's tooltip.

li.heading: Fill suggested and what the trade leaves

points.li: Fill suggested, at the foot of either screen, puts the marked goods into the trade within the silver both sides have: the buys first, each need answered once by the cheapest for what it gives, then the sales as far as the trader's silver goes. Rows you set yourself stay as they are, and their silver counts first. Clear suggested takes it back out.
Under each side's silver: what it has after the trade, red when it runs short.
At the foot of a trade at home: the days the colony's food lasts now and after the trade. A caravan's own days of food and its mass after the trade are the game's, at the top.
No letters, and no messages but the game's own: it is all on the trade screen. Not in gift mode; where the trader deals in favor, only the marks for need.

li.heading: Market prices and the colony's record

points.li: Point at a good in Rimfolk's window, or at either price on the game's screen, for its card, beside the mouse on the other side from the tooltip: the colony's own last prices for it (what it last got and paid a piece, to whom and how long ago, and the best of the last 15 days), and with Vanilla Trading Expanded its market.

The colony's trade record notes each silver trade as it goes through: what was sold and bought, to whom and at what price a piece. It keeps the last 5 trades of each good and 50 goods, the good traded longest ago going first; gifts, people and animals are left out.

Vanilla Trading Expanded keeps one price a day of every good its market trades. The card shows the market value now against its usual worth and against its average of the last 30 days, its change over the last 7 and 30 days, its lowest and highest of the last 60 days with a drawn line of them, and the news that last moved it.

A good whose market value moved notably (a tenth up or down in 7 days, or a fifth in 30) has a small line beside its name, green rising and red falling, its card on it. The price change sort in the Sort by menus puts the biggest moves first, up or down; it is offered only with Vanilla Trading Expanded.

Vanilla Trading Expanded moves a price by the colony's own trades too: every three days, with a chance of the market worth the colony traded of a good over 1,000 silver (certain from 1,000), down for a sale and up for a purchase. The card and the mark's tooltip say in words whether this trade is likely to move it and which way; a trade against what the colony traded of it lately evens it out.

The marks' tooltips gain the market's reasons: a sale at the highest of 60 days, or of a good falling fast, is better made now; so is a buy at the lowest of 60 days, or of a good rising fast. At the other end, what can wait may do better with a later trader. Reasons only: the marks themselves are the colony's needs.

The Market button on the silver row opens a window of the trade's goods: against usual, 7 days, 30 days, a line of 60 days, last sold and last bought, each column sorted by a click, the biggest movers first. Without Vanilla Trading Expanded it shows the colony's record alone, with the best of the last 15 days, the goods traded most lately first.

li.heading: With Vanilla Trading Expanded or Trade Helper

points.li: Vanilla Trading Expanded draws nothing on the trade screen. Its world market's price against a good's usual worth counts in the best deal and the marks, so a good in demand fetches a good price and one in surplus is a bargain, and the tooltip names it. A contract on its terminal keeps the goods it asks for, and makes them worth buying where this trader's price leaves the reward a fifth ahead; the colony's own contracts are worth buying here when the trader asks less than they offer. The silver in its banks shows at the foot. Its own settings are on the page of your other mods: its market and contracts, and its price history (the market part of the card and the window, the trend line, the price change sort, what a trade does to the price, the marks' reasons).

Trade Helper widens the game's screen for a side panel of its own (a wish list, and lists of what is bought and sold), so it shows when you switch to the game's screen. Rimfolk draws nothing there; with it loaded the silver after the trade is left to its lists.
